title: Emulated: The Data for Fully Autonomous Software Engineers and Companies — Joseph Wang

primary.label: AI Data Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The simulated environments are designed for software builders and infrastructure engineers. The talk describes provisioning VPCs, subnets, security groups, deployment systems, and monitoring—core developer platform concerns. The domain expertise they leverage comes from infrastructure and platform companies like Modal and Supabase.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: They explicitly state they are not exclusively focused on infrastructure and plan to scale horizontally to other domains. The containerized-company approach is domain-agnostic in principle, with infrastructure as the first vertical.

summary: Joseph Wang (CEO) and co-founder Sid Patlollu (CTO) present Emulated, a data lab building high-fidelity training environments for AI agents that must operate production infrastructure. Speaking at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026, they trace a model capability gap—agents excel at application-layer tasks but fail on infrastructure reasoning (MVCC corruption, distributed node failures, clock skew, blast radius)—to a data gap. Current benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, and others referred to in the talk as "Deep Sweep" and "Frontier Code") only test codebase-level tasks over 50-100 turns producing thousand-line PRs, missing the full engineering context: customer interaction, performance testing, multi-year infrastructure ownership. Emulated's approach containerizes entire software engineering companies with organizational context—projects, incidents, postmortems, customer conversations—and forces agents to handle scale-only failures while serving live traffic. They demonstrate an etcd consensus cluster environment showing surrounding context including tickets, deployment systems, failing nodes, and monitoring. They argue single-node sandboxes cannot simulate real cloud infrastructure requiring VPCs, subnets, security groups, APIs with throttling, deployment systems, health monitoring, DNS, billing, and scheduling. Their proposed solution is a multi-node sandbox with real cloud resources—a cloud-in-a-box. They acknowledge challenges including hours-long startup times, cost management, and a persistent sim-to-real gap. They start with infrastructure because domain expertise drives data quality and infra problem statements are clearest, then plan to scale lessons horizontally to other domains.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a coherent argument chain: the data gap thesis (AI concept) explains why agents lack infrastructure reasoning capabilities, which manifests as failures in blast radius analysis, MVCC corruption handling, and scale-only failure management (SE concepts). The benchmark scope limitations (AI concept) quantify this gap—50-100 turn tasks producing thousand-line PRs versus the full infrastructure ownership lifecycle (SE concept). Emulated's containerized company environments with multi-node sandbox architecture (SE concepts) are the proposed solution, grounded in the principle that domain expertise drives data quality (AI concept). The sim-to-real gap (SE concept) and post-training pipeline constraints (AI concept) represent the practical challenges that bound this solution. The vertical-to-horizontal scaling strategy (AI concept) provides the roadmap for translating infrastructure-specific lessons to broader domains. Together, these concepts define a new category of AI data engineering—synthetic environment generation for RL training—that bridges the gap between benchmark performance and real-world agent autonomy.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 and published on YouTube on July 31, 2026. It occurs during a period of rapid evolution and acknowledged insufficiency in agentic coding benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified has been retired, SWE-bench Pro's public split is partially broken, Terminal-Bench 2.1 is approaching saturation at 74-84%, and Frontier-Bench v0.1 has just launched. The broader AI engineering community is grappling with the gap between benchmark performance and real-world agent reliability, particularly for infrastructure and long-horizon tasks. Emulated emerges as an approach attempting to close this gap through higher-fidelity training environments rather than model architecture improvements, positioning synthetic environment generation as a distinct discipline within AI data engineering.
takeaways: Model capability gaps in infrastructure work stem from data gaps—current training data does not capture production-scale infrastructure complexity.
Existing benchmarks like SweBench Pro and Terminal Bench only test codebase-level tasks over 50-100 turns, missing customer interaction, performance testing, and long-term infrastructure ownership.
Emulated containerizes entire software engineering companies including organizational context, incidents, customer conversations, and scale-only failures like network partitions and clock skew.
Single-node sandboxes break down when agents must provision real cloud resources—VPCs, subnets, security groups, APIs with throttling, deployment systems, billing, and monitoring.
Their proposed multi-node sandbox provides real cloud infrastructure access, essentially a cloud-in-a-box, to enable higher-fidelity training environments.
Starting with infrastructure because domain expertise drives data quality and infra problem statements are clearest; lessons translate horizontally to other domains.
Key challenges include hours-long stack startup times, cost management, and a sim-to-real gap that persists even with real resources.
They are actively recruiting distributed systems engineers and people who have trained models to help expand fidelity across more domains.

concepts.name: Data gap thesis for agent capability
concepts.explanation: The argument that model capability gaps in infrastructure work stem from a training data gap—current training data does not capture production-scale infrastructure complexity—rather than from model architecture limitations. This reframes the problem from model improvement to data engineering.
concepts.importance: Foundational premise of Emulated's entire approach; drives the decision to build better training environments rather than modify model architectures.

concepts.name: Agentic coding benchmark scope limitations
concepts.explanation: Current agentic coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE, FrontierSWE) only test codebase-level tasks over 50-100 turns producing thousand-line PRs, missing infrastructure work, customer interaction, and long-term ownership. Web verification confirms SWE-bench Pro has 1,865 problems with top models below 25%, and Terminal-Bench has 89 tasks with frontier models below 65%.
concepts.importance: Core motivating argument for why higher-fidelity training environments are needed; establishes the baseline that Emulated improves upon.

concepts.name: Synthetic environment generation for RL training
concepts.explanation: Creating high-fidelity simulated environments—including organizational context, incidents, and scale-only failures—for reinforcement learning training of AI agents. Emulated's core product category, described on their homepage as RL environments for real-world engineering complexity.
concepts.importance: Defines Emulated's product category and approach to closing the data gap through environment engineering rather than data labeling.

concepts.name: Domain expertise as data quality driver
concepts.explanation: The principle that domain expertise informs how high-quality training data can be. Emulated starts with infrastructure because the founders' expertise in network infrastructure and distributed databases ensures data quality in that domain.
concepts.importance: Strategic rationale for Emulated's domain selection and a generalizable principle for training data engineering across domains.

concepts.name: Post-training pipeline integration constraints
concepts.explanation: The challenge of fitting multi-node sandbox environments with hours-long startup times into post-training rollout pipelines that have strict time and cost budgets. Full infrastructure stack startup (e.g., AWS Lambda) can take hours, which is impractical for rollout cycles.
concepts.importance: Practical engineering constraint that shapes how Emulated's environments can be consumed by training pipelines and informs design trade-offs.

concepts.name: Vertical-to-horizontal domain scaling strategy
concepts.explanation: Strategy of going deep vertically on infrastructure first—where domain expertise is strongest and problem statements are clearest—then translating lessons horizontally to other domains. Infrastructure companies like Modal and Supabase have clear user needs (GPU sandboxes with low latency, low cost, no mid-training failures).
concepts.importance: Defines Emulated's roadmap and provides a transferable framework for applying data engineering expertise to new domains.

concepts.name: Low-fidelity industry emulation critique
concepts.explanation: Wang's critique that the industry's current approach to emulating the real world for agent training is 'incredibly contrived and low fidelity,' motivating the need for full-fidelity environments that include entire company contexts rather than isolated codebases.
concepts.importance: Frames the competitive landscape and the gap Emulated aims to fill relative to existing benchmark and training approaches.

concepts.name: Agent autonomy for long-horizon infrastructure work
concepts.explanation: The goal of increasing AI agent reliability and autonomy for long-horizon infrastructure tasks that currently require human engineers with deep domain expertise. When mission-critical services like DynamoDB fail, large portions of the internet go down, underscoring the stakes.
concepts.importance: Defines the downstream application that Emulated's data engineering serves and the real-world impact of the capability gap.

concepts.name: Multi-node sandbox architecture
concepts.explanation: A sandbox architecture spanning multiple networked nodes with real cloud resources, as opposed to single-node containers. Emulated proposes this to enable agents to encounter distributed system failures, network partitions, and cross-node resource provisioning that single-node sandboxes cannot simulate.
concepts.importance: Central to Emulated's proposed solution for closing the sim-to-real gap in agent training environments; defines the infrastructure requirement for high-fidelity simulation.

concepts.name: Containerized company environments
concepts.explanation: Emulated places entire software engineering companies into containerized environments, including organizational context like projects, incidents, customer conversations, and postmortems, so agents must reason about the full engineering context beyond source code.
concepts.importance: Core methodology of Emulated's data lab approach; defines what makes their training data higher fidelity than existing benchmarks that only test codebase-level diffs.

concepts.name: Blast radius analysis
concepts.explanation: The scope of impact when a component in a distributed system fails. Used as an example of infrastructure reasoning that agents currently cannot perform—understanding which downstream services are affected when a node or service goes down.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the kind of infrastructure-level reasoning that current agent training data does not capture, motivating Emulated's approach.

concepts.name: Cloud resource provisioning pipeline
concepts.explanation: The process of setting up real cloud infrastructure components—VPCs, subnets, security groups, front-end APIs with throttling and authentication, deployment systems with rollback, health monitoring, DNS, billing, admin consoles, and scheduling. The talk argues these cannot fit in a single-node sandbox.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates the complexity gap between current sandbox evaluations and real production infrastructure, justifying the multi-node approach.

concepts.name: Distributed consensus (etcd)
concepts.explanation: Consensus protocols like etcd that manage state across distributed nodes. Used as a demonstration environment showing surrounding context: tickets, postmortems, deployment systems, failing nodes, and live traffic monitoring.
concepts.importance: Concrete example of the kind of infrastructure system agents must learn to operate, including failure modes like flapping nodes and lagging learners.

concepts.name: MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)
concepts.explanation: A database concurrency control mechanism mentioned as an infrastructure reasoning challenge where agents struggle, particularly around corruption risks under concurrent access patterns in distributed databases.
concepts.importance: Specific example of the infrastructure knowledge gap in current AI agents, grounding the capability gap argument in a concrete technical concept.

concepts.name: Scale-only failures
concepts.explanation: Failures that only manifest at production scale—network partitions between distributed nodes, data corruption, clock skew, flapping nodes, and lagging learners. These cannot be reproduced in single-node or small-scale sandbox environments.
concepts.importance: Defines the class of problems that Emulated's multi-node sandbox is specifically designed to expose agents to during training.

concepts.name: Infrastructure ownership lifecycle
concepts.explanation: The full lifecycle of owning production infrastructure over months or years, including customer interaction, performance testing, incident response, and long-term maintenance. Current benchmarks capture none of this temporal context.
concepts.importance: Motivates the need for containerized company environments that include temporal and organizational context beyond codebase diffs.

concepts.name: Sim-to-real gap in infrastructure simulation
concepts.explanation: The persistent gap between simulated training environments and real production systems. Even with real cloud resources, the gap remains because real customer traffic, scale-only problems, and multi-year ownership cannot be fully replicated.
concepts.importance: Central challenge that Emulated acknowledges but does not claim to fully solve; frames their work as fidelity improvement rather than complete emulation.

concepts.name: Rolling deployment with health checks
concepts.explanation: A deployment strategy that gradually replaces old service versions while monitoring health, maintaining the ability to roll back. Included in the containerized company environment context as part of deployment systems agents must manage.
concepts.importance: Part of the operational infrastructure context that distinguishes full engineering work from codebase-level tasks tested by current benchmarks.

sections.title: Introduction and Mission
sections.summary: Joseph Wang and co-founder Sid introduce Emulated as a data lab for increasing AI agent reliability and autonomy. They preview topics including simulating companies in sandboxes, multi-node distributed clusters, and post-training pipeline implications. Their backgrounds in network infrastructure, distributed databases, and sandbox infra inform their perspective on mission-critical systems.

sections.title: The Data and Capability Gap
sections.summary: They identify a model capability gap: agents handle application-layer tasks well but struggle with infrastructure reasoning like MVCC and its corruption risks. They trace this to a data gap, noting current benchmarks (SweBench Pro, Terminal Bench, Frontier Code, Deep Sweep) only test codebase-level tasks over 50-100 turns, missing customer interaction, performance testing, and multi-year infrastructure ownership.

sections.title: Containerized Company Environments
sections.summary: Emulated places entire software engineering companies into containerized environments with organizational context—projects, incidents, customer conversations. Agents must handle scale-only issues like network failures, data corruption, and clock skew while orchestrating distributed clusters and reasoning about blast radius. An etcd consensus cluster example shows the full environment: tickets, postmortems, deployments, failing nodes, and live traffic monitoring.

sections.title: Limits of Single-Node Sandboxes
sections.summary: They argue single-node sandboxes break down for real infrastructure work. Building a cloud service requires resource provisioning (VPCs, subnets, security groups), front-end APIs with throttling and authentication, deployment systems with rollback, health monitoring, DNS, billing, admin consoles, and scheduling—none of which fit neatly into a single containerized sandbox.

sections.title: Multi-Node Sandbox and Call to Action
sections.summary: Their proposed solution is a multi-node sandbox with real cloud infrastructure access—a cloud-in-a-box. They acknowledge challenges: hours-long startup for stacks like AWS Lambda, cost management, and persistent sim-to-real gap. They share these challenges openly to recruit distributed systems engineers and model trainers, inviting people with niche infrastructure opinions to collaborate.

sections.title: Why It's Called Emulated and Domain Strategy
sections.summary: Wang explains the name 'Emulated' reflects their goal of emulating the real world with full fidelity—not just systems but entire companies. In Q&A, they clarify they are not exclusively focused on infra but starting there because domain expertise drives data quality and infra problem statements are clearest (e.g., Modal users want GPU sandboxes with low latency, low cost, no mid-training failures). They note lessons from going deep vertically on infrastructure translate horizontally to other domains, and they are exploring scaling out that way before closing the talk.

demonstrations: Example of an etcd consensus cluster environment showing surrounding context: tickets, postmortems, deployment systems, failing nodes, and live traffic monitoring.
Walkthrough of building a cloud service from a single piece of software through resource provisioning, front-end API, deployment, health monitoring, DNS, billing, and scheduling.
limitations: Single-node sandboxes cannot simulate real cloud resource provisioning like EC2 or Cloud Run.
Sim-to-real gap persists even with real resources—still need live customer traffic and scale-only problems.
Hours-long startup times for full infrastructure stacks are difficult to fit into post-training rollouts.
Current benchmarks do not capture multi-month or multi-year infrastructure ownership.
Cost management for multi-node sandbox environments remains an open challenge.
Industry's current emulation of the real world is incredibly contrived and low fidelity.
quantitativeClaims: Current benchmark tasks run 50 to 100 turns and produce a couple thousand-line PR.
Spinning up the entire stack for something like AWS Lambda takes hours.
DynamoDB going down took down US East 1 and half the internet.

organization.name: Emulated
organization.summary: Emulated is a data lab that builds RL environments simulating production systems to train AI models for real-world engineering complexity. Their approach involves containerizing entire software engineering companies with organizational context, incidents, and scale-only failures using multi-node sandboxes with real cloud resources. Founded by Joseph Wang (CEO) and Sid Patlollu (CTO), the company is in early/stealth stage as of 2026-08-23. Their official website is https://emulated.so/ with contact at founders@emulated.so. The homepage describes their technical bet that models need access to more challenging problems like migrating systems from AWS to GCP, debugging distributed system failures, building serverless runtimes, and building container orchestrators.

technologies.label: High-fidelity simulation environments for RL-based agent training
technologies.primary: Synthetic environment generation for RL training
technologies.summary: Emulated's core technology category: generating high-fidelity simulation environments that containerize entire software engineering companies with organizational context—projects, incidents, customer conversations, postmortems—and expose agents to scale-only failures like network partitions, clock skew, and data corruption while serving live traffic. The approach uses multi-node sandboxes with real cloud resources (a cloud-in-a-box) to close the sim-to-real gap that existing benchmarks cannot address. The founders start with infrastructure because their domain expertise ensures data quality, and plan to scale lessons horizontally to other domains.
technologies.role: Central technology presented; defines Emulated's product category and approach to closing the data gap in AI agent training for infrastructure work

technologies.label: Agentic coding benchmarks
technologies.summary: Existing agentic coding benchmark suites that test AI agents on codebase-level tasks over 50-100 turns producing thousand-line PRs. The video systematically critiques SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE (referred to as 'Deep Sweep'), and FrontierSWE (referred to as 'Frontier Code') as insufficient for capturing infrastructure-level engineering work, customer interaction, performance testing, and multi-year infrastructure ownership. Web verification confirms these benchmarks exist with the described scope limitations, and a July 2026 Backgrind article independently corroborates that the benchmark landscape is evolving rapidly with several benchmarks retiring or saturating.
technologies.role: Existing technologies critiqued as insufficient; establish the capability and data gap that motivates Emulated's approach to higher-fidelity training environments

technologies.label: Distributed consensus and infrastructure reasoning systems
technologies.summary: Distributed consensus systems and infrastructure reasoning concepts that represent the class of problems AI agents currently cannot handle. The video demonstrates an etcd consensus cluster as a training environment with full organizational context—tickets, postmortems, deployment systems, failing nodes, and live traffic monitoring. It discusses MVCC corruption risks, blast radius analysis, and scale-only failures (network partitions, clock skew, flapping nodes, lagging learners) as specific infrastructure reasoning challenges that motivate the need for higher-fidelity training environments.
technologies.role: Demonstration environment and concrete examples of the infrastructure reasoning gap in current AI agents that Emulated aims to close

technologies.label: Cloud infrastructure provisioning and sandbox platforms
technologies.summary: Cloud infrastructure provisioning pipelines and sandbox platforms that represent the real-world complexity agents must learn to manage. The video argues that building a cloud service requires provisioning VPCs, subnets, security groups, front-end APIs with throttling and authentication, deployment systems with rollback, health monitoring, DNS, billing, admin consoles, and scheduling—none of which fit into single-node sandboxes. Modal and Supabase are cited as example infrastructure companies with clear user needs, and the hours-long startup time for full stacks like AWS Lambda is identified as a key practical challenge for integrating these environments into post-training pipelines.
technologies.role: Defines the infrastructure complexity that single-node sandboxes cannot capture and that motivates Emulated's multi-node cloud-in-a-box approach; Modal and Supabase illustrate why infrastructure is the optimal starting domain

prerequisites: Familiarity with distributed systems concepts including consensus protocols, MVCC, network partitions, and clock skew
Understanding of cloud infrastructure provisioning (VPCs, subnets, security groups, deployment systems, DNS, billing)
Knowledge of post-training pipelines and sandbox-based agent evaluation
Awareness of current agentic coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench) and their scope limitations
outcomes: Explain why current AI agent benchmarks fail to capture infrastructure-level engineering work and trace the capability gap to a training data gap
Identify the fidelity gap between single-node sandbox evaluation and real production infrastructure complexity including multi-node failures and blast radius
Describe how containerized company environments with organizational context (tickets, postmortems, incidents, customer conversations) can train agents on end-to-end infrastructure tasks
Evaluate design considerations for multi-node sandboxes that provision real cloud resources, including startup time, cost management, and sim-to-real gap persistence
Articulate why domain expertise matters for training data quality and why infrastructure is a practical starting vertical for company-level simulation with horizontal scaling potential
challengeSeeds: Design a containerized environment simulating a small infrastructure company with at least three services, including incident tickets and deployment logs, and identify which organizational context elements most impact agent training quality
Compare single-node vs multi-node sandbox fidelity for a specific infrastructure task such as a rolling deployment with health checks and quantify the sim-to-real gap for each approach
Propose a cost-efficient strategy for reducing hours-long infrastructure stack startup times to fit within post-training rollout time budgets without sacrificing fidelity

Select a non-infrastructure domain and apply Emulated's vertical-then-horizontal scaling strategy: identify the domain expertise needed, the clearest problem statements, and the hardest scale-only failures to simulate
